findings.claim: examiners deduct marks for descriptions that simply state what happens without explaining why it matters
findings.truth: Edexcel marks positively; nothing is deducted. The spec's command-word table defines Explain as needing reasoning or justification, with linked marking points, so an unreasoned point simply does not gain the mark.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Explain, 2 to 4 marks)

findings.claim: Your specification identifies four key benefits of structuring programs using subprograms.
findings.truth: The spec does not enumerate any benefits. 1.1.2 says only 'understand the benefits of using subprograms'. The four named in the lesson are a teaching list, not a spec list.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.2

findings.claim: Name the four benefits of using subprograms listed in the specification.
findings.truth: Same as F2: the spec lists no benefits. The flashcard should not tell a student the four are a spec list.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.2

findings.claim: 'Identify two sub-problems...' typed as '1 mark - Identify', with a mark scheme that then argues with itself: '1 mark for each valid sub-problem (up to 2 marks for this question in exam context, but listed as 1-mark Identify type - accept any one clearly valid sub-problem for 1 mark)'.
findings.truth: Edexcel's taxonomy gives Identify 1 mark for each item identified. A question asking for two items is a 2-mark question. The tariff label and the mark scheme must agree.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Identify, 1 mark for each)

findings.claim: In a flowchart showing a loop, an arrow curves back upward from the "No" exit of the diamond to an earlier process step.
findings.truth: The loop-back arrow leaves whichever exit continues the loop. In the standard condition-controlled (while) flowchart the decision tests the continue-condition, so the Yes exit loops back and the No exit leaves the loop. Stated as a blanket rule the claim is wrong and would make a student draw the loop the wrong way round.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2.1 and Appendix 2 flowchart symbols; standard while-loop flowchart form

findings.claim: revision tip: 'write out all six arithmetic operators and four relational operators from memory'
findings.truth: The spec names seven arithmetic operators (addition, subtraction, division, multiplication, modulus, integer division, exponentiation) and six relational operators (equal to, less than, greater than, not equal to, less than or equal to, greater than or equal to). The key fact next to the tip correctly lists seven and six, so the tip also contradicts its own paragraph.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2.3

findings.claim: Examiners award marks for correct logic, not correct syntax.
findings.truth: True for pseudocode answers only, because of the spec footnote. Paper 1 also carries Write and Amend items that require program code in the Programming Language Subset, i.e. Python 3, where notation does matter. As a blanket claim it misleads.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2 footnote on pseudocode; spec Appendix 1 (Write, Amend); spec section on the Programming Language Subset and Python 3

findings.claim: 'Write a plain-English algorithm that displays Distinction / Merit / Pass' typed as '4 marks - Describe'.
findings.truth: The task is to write an algorithm, which is the Write command word (1 to 6 marks). Describe means giving an account, and teaches the wrong exam technique for this task.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy

findings.claim: 'Write a plain-English algorithm ... stopping when they enter 0' typed as '6 marks - Complete an Algorithm'.
findings.truth: 'Complete an Algorithm' is not an Edexcel command word, and nothing is given to complete. The stem is a Write task; Write carries 1 to 6 marks, so 6 marks is valid once relabelled.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (only the listed verbs are used in question papers)

findings.claim: 'State the difference between count-controlled repetition and condition-controlled repetition.' typed as '2 marks - Describe'.
findings.truth: State carries 1 mark for each item recalled, so a 2-mark State question conflicts with the taxonomy. The displayed tariff (2 marks - Describe) is itself valid, so this is a stem/label mismatch rather than an impossible tariff.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Give/State/Name, 1 mark for each)

findings.claim: Algorithms can be written in three forms: as a flowchart, as pseudocode, or as actual program code. The lesson never names the program code language.
findings.truth: The lesson is correct that Edexcel pseudocode is informal plain English, and it correctly avoids teaching another board's reference language. But Edexcel expects students to be familiar with and use the Programming Language Subset, and the qualification uses Python 3 as its programming language. Options: (a) leave as is, since nothing stated is false; (b) name Python 3 and the Programming Language Subset in the opening paragraph so the third form is not left abstract for a whole unit.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2 (students expected to be familiar with and use the PLS); spec section on adopting Python 3; spec Paper 2 overview
findings.ruling: Named Python 3 / the Programming Language Subset as the program-code form in the opening paragraph.

findings.claim: examiners report that many students give vague definitions that could apply to more than one type
findings.truth: No examiner report is cited and none can be verified. The teaching point stands on its own: a definition that fits more than one error type does not gain the mark.
findings.evidence: no published source; claim is unattributable

findings.claim: a statement of fact alone earns only half the marks
findings.truth: Invented mark-scheme arithmetic. Edexcel publishes no such half-marks rule. Explain items require reasoning, so an unreasoned statement does not meet the demand of the question.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Explain)

findings.claim: 'Show the steps a binary search would take to find Patel' typed as '4 marks - Complete a Trace Table'.
findings.truth: No trace table is supplied and none is asked for, and 'Show' is not an Edexcel command word. The task is to give an account of the search steps, which is Describe (2 to 4 marks). The worked steps themselves are correct: Khan, Singh, Martin, Patel, four comparisons, floor midpoint convention consistent with the lesson.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy; recomputation of the search

findings.claim: Very fast for large sorted datasets (at most log2(n) comparisons).
findings.truth: The exact worst case is floor(log2 n) + 1 comparisons, so for an exact power of two the stated formula is one short. The two numeric claims in the lesson are right (1,000 items in at most 10; one million in at most 20), and Edexcel does not assess complexity, so the approximation is not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: recomputation

findings.claim: 'Complete the truth table for the expression NOT A.' typed as '2 marks - Convert'.
findings.truth: Convert means changing information from one symbolic representation to another. Filling in a supplied table is the Complete command word (2 to 6 marks).
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy

findings.claim: 'Complete the full truth table for the expression A OR (NOT B)' typed as '4 marks - Complete a Trace Table'.
findings.truth: It is a truth table, not a trace table. The two are different artefacts and a student told to build a trace table for a Boolean expression will produce the wrong thing. The answer key itself is correct (T, F, T, T).
findings.evidence: spec 1.3.1 and 1.2.4; recomputation of all four rows

findings.claim: 'Write this as a logical expression and complete a truth table for it with inputs A, B and C' typed as '6 marks - Complete an Algorithm'.
findings.truth: No algorithm is involved; the task is completing a truth table. Complete carries 2 to 6 marks, so 6 marks is valid once relabelled. The expression A AND (B OR C) and the 6-mark split in the scheme are correct.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy; spec 1.3.1

findings.claim: examiners award marks for intermediate working as well as the final output
findings.truth: An invented mark-scheme claim; Edexcel publishes no such rule for truth-table items. The advice to show intermediate columns is still sound on method grounds.
findings.evidence: no published source; claim is unattributable

findings.claim: The mark scheme for 'A OR (NOT B)' allocates marks twice: 1 for the NOT B column plus 1 for the OR column, then 1 for row 1 plus 1 for row 2, then 'All four outputs correct = 4 marks'.
findings.truth: Three competing allocations for the same 4 marks. Each sums to 4, so no student is misled about the tariff, but the scheme reads as three schemes stacked. Not worth an edit on its own.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency

summary: Every algorithm, trace and truth table in this unit recomputes correctly: the sum-to-4 and factorial traces, both binary search worked examples (floor midpoint convention consistent throughout), the bubble sort pass states, the merge sort split and merge of [7, 2, 9, 4], all two- and three-input truth tables, the 999/29/10/20 comparison counts, and every knowledge check and match key. The findings are all in the exam layer: five invented examiner or mark-scheme claims, two false claims about what the specification lists, and eight practice questions whose command-word labels do not exist in Edexcel's taxonomy or do not match the task set (including two truth tables labelled trace tables). The lesson correctly teaches Edexcel pseudocode as informal plain English and does not import another board's reference language.
